# 2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado

The **2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado** was a long-tracked and destructive tornado that struck Central Alabama on the afternoon of April 27, 2011. Occurring as part of the 2011 Super Outbreak, the largest tornado outbreak in United States history, this storm was rated EF3 on the Enhanced Fujita scale. The tornado tracked for over 72 miles (116 km) through Greene, Hale, and Bibb counties, reaching a maximum path width of one mile (1.6 km) and estimated peak wind speeds of 145 mph (233 km/h). The storm resulted in seven fatalities and at least 50 injuries, causing extensive structural damage to homes, businesses, and the Eoline Volunteer Fire Department .

## Meteorological synopsis

The tornado occurred during the April 25–28, 2011 tornado outbreak, a historic severe weather event that produced 362 confirmed tornadoes across the southern, midwestern, and northeastern United States. April 27 was the peak of the outbreak, characterized by a volatile atmospheric environment with high levels of wind shear and instability .

The Sawyerville–Eoline tornado was one of 29 confirmed tornadoes to impact Central Alabama on that day. It touched down at approximately 5:30 p.m. CDT (22:30 UTC) and remained on the ground for nearly one hour and a half, dissipating at 6:55 p.m. CDT (23:55 UTC). The storm was one of several long-track supercells that traversed the state during the afternoon and evening "second wave" of the outbreak .

## Storm path and impact

The tornado followed a northeasterly path, affecting rural communities and forested areas across three counties. The National Weather Service (NWS) in Birmingham conducted damage surveys to determine the track and intensity of the storm .

### Greene County
The tornado first touched down in extreme southwest Greene County, near the Tombigbee River, west of the Tishabee community. The initial damage occurred along County Road 69 near Head Drive. In this early stage, the tornado was rated EF1 but quickly intensified to EF2 status as it moved northeast across rural areas north of Forkland. Damage in Greene County included the destruction or damage of at least four mobile homes, three outbuildings, and two churches. Numerous trees were also downed in this area. Two minor injuries were reported in the county before the tornado crossed the Black Warrior River and entered Hale County .

### Hale County
Upon entering Hale County west of Sawyerville, the tornado intensified significantly. As it crossed Alabama State Route 14 just north of Sawyerville, the tornado reached EF3 intensity with winds estimated at 145 mph. The storm continued northeast, crossing County Roads 18 and 21, Alabama State Route 69 south of Harper Hill, and County Road 29 east of Ingram .

This segment of the path experienced the most severe impacts in terms of casualties. Extensive structural damage occurred, with numerous mobile homes and single-family residences destroyed. One church was also destroyed in this area. Thousands of trees were snapped or uprooted along the path. Six of the seven fatalities associated with this tornado occurred in Hale County, along with at least 40 injuries .

### Bibb County and Eoline
The tornado moved from Hale County into the Talladega National Forest near Ingram, maintaining its strength as it crossed into Bibb County. It caused significant damage to timber within the national forest before approaching the community of Eoline.

In Eoline, the tornado inflicted significant structural damage consistent with an EF3 rating. Approximately one dozen mobile homes and single-family houses were destroyed, and numerous others sustained varying degrees of damage. The Eoline Volunteer Fire Department building was destroyed by the tornado. Twelve people survived the direct hit by taking shelter in the hallway of the fire station. However, one fatality occurred in Eoline involving a person in a vehicle near the destroyed fire department. At least 10 other injuries were noted in this area .

The tornado continued northeast, crossing Alabama State Route 5 south of West Blocton. By this point, the storm had weakened slightly to an EF2 rating with winds estimated at 125 mph. Several mobile homes and site-built homes near County Road 26 were destroyed or heavily damaged. The tornado continued to down thousands of trees as it weakened further, eventually lifting just northeast of the Marvel community near the Shelby County and Bibb County line .

## Casualties and damage summary

The National Weather Service confirmed seven fatalities and 50 injuries directly attributed to the tornado. Six deaths occurred in Hale County, and one death occurred in Bibb County .

**Summary of Statistics:**
* **EF Rating:** EF3
* **Estimated Peak Winds:** 145 mph (233 km/h)
* **Path Length:** 72.13 miles (116.08 km)
* **Maximum Width:** 1,760 yards (1.0 mile)
* **Fatalities:** 7
* **Injuries:** 50

The storm destroyed the Eoline Volunteer Fire Department and another business in Eoline. Across the entire path, hundreds of structures were impacted, and thousands of trees were downed, contributing to power outages and road closures in the region .

## Aftermath and recovery

Following the tornado, relief efforts were coordinated by local emergency management agencies and community organizations. The Greensboro Recreational Center in Greensboro, Alabama, served as a distribution point for food, clothing, and household items for victims .

The destruction caused by the 2011 outbreak, including the Sawyerville–Eoline tornado, highlighted the vulnerability of rural communities in the region, particularly those relying on mobile homes. In the years following the disaster, local officials and federal representatives prioritized the construction of community storm shelters.

In 2023 and 2024, Hale County secured federal grant money, facilitated by U.S. Representative Terri Sewell, to construct new community storm shelters. These efforts were driven by the history of severe weather in the area, including the 2011 tornado and subsequent storms in 2022 and 2023. Four new shelters were planned for the communities of Akron, Greensboro, Moundville, and Sawyerville to provide safe refuge for residents during future severe weather events . By September 2024, shelters in Akron and Sawyerville were operational, with others in Moundville and Greensboro in various stages of completion .

						Event Summary for Central Alabama

						As part of a system which wreaked havoc across the eastern half of the United States (April 25-28), the following is an account of the tornado outbreak of April 27th, 2011, in Central Alabama.

						National Weather Service meteorologists completed the assessment of storm damage from this tragically historic day of tornadic activity and severe weather across Central Alabama on Wednesday, April 27th.  Nationally recognized storm damage experts assisted us in examining the locations of the most extreme damage to ensure we provided the most accurate assessment of this event as possible.

						In total, there were 29 confirmed tornadoes in Central Alabama on this day, and 62 confirmed tornadoes across the State of Alabama.

						Click on the numbered boxes on the map below to view more detailed information about each tornado track.

						The tornado damage swaths as depicted in the image above, and on the individual tornado links, are an estimate of the damage widths along the track.  In other words, the track width may not represent the actual damage in all locations, as we interpolate the values between actual surveyed damage points.  These maps are soley for the purpose of showing the general track of each tornado.  Remember, tornadoes do not always move in straight lines, and the intensity does not remain constant.  It is also possible to have other thunderstorm wind-related damage in close proximity to the tornado tracks from such features as inflow and rear flank downdrafts, which can produce tornado-like damage.  For a satellite image of the tornado tracks, click here.

						For comprehensive GIS information, including ESRI Shapefiles and Google Earth KMZ files of tornado paths, storm survey points, and tracks of all 62 tornadoes, click on the link below:

						Pertinent Geographic Information Systems (GIS) Data from the April 27th, 2011 Outbreak

						Important Note: The Shapefiles and KMLs are experimental data.

						To tell the story of April 27, 2011, one has to recognize that there were two distinct waves of widespread severe weather in Central Alabama. The first wave of severe storms moved through during the early morning hours across northern portions of Central Alabama in the form of a Quasi-Linear Covective System (QLCS).  This  intense line of thunderstorms produced not only widespread damaging straight line winds in the areas of Moody, Pell City and Riverside, but numerous strong tornadoes.  The table below is an account of the tornadoes caused by the QLCS:

						Central Alabama April 27th Statistics

						- April 27th was one of the largest super-tornado outbreaks in Central Alabama history.

						- April 25th-28th was one of the largest super-tornado outbreaks in US history.

						- There were 29 confirmed tornadoes in Central Alabama on April 27th. 62 tornadoes occurred across the state.

						- The combined tornado damage path length in Central Alabama was 691.02 miles.

						- Sixteen of the tornadoes had damage path lengths over 10 miles long.

						- Eight of the tornadoes had damage path lengths over 25 miles long.

						- Eight tornadoes either started or ended outside Central Alabama.

						- There were at least 1998 injuries reported and 240 people lost their lives.

						-  Tornado Watch 225  was in effect from 226 am CDT until 8 am CDT.

						- Tornado Watch 230 was in effect from 812 am CDT until 2 pm CDT.

						- PDS Tornado Watch 235 was in effect from 145 pm CDT until 10 pm CDT.

						- PDS Tornado Watch 241 was in effect from 552 pm CDT until 1 am CDT.

						- Tornado Watch 245 was in effect from 942 pm CDT until 2 am CDT.

						- NWS BMX issued 49 Tornado Warnings.

[](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado&action=edit&section=0&oldformat=true)On the afternoon of April 27, 2011, a large, long-tracked, and destructive low-end EF3 tornado, known as the **Sawyerville–Eoline tornado**,[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1) moved across [Central Alabama](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Central_Alabama "Central Alabama"), in the [United States](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/United_States "United States"), moving through areas near numerous towns along its 72.1-mile (116.0 km) track, including [Tishabee](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tishabee,_Alabama "Tishabee, Alabama"), [Sawyerville](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Sawyerville,_Alabama "Sawyerville, Alabama"), [Havana](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Havana,_Alabama "Havana, Alabama") and [Eoline](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Eoline,_Alabama "Eoline, Alabama"). The tornado killed seven, injured 52, and impacted hundreds of structures. It occurred as part of the [largest tornado outbreak in modern history](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Super_Outbreak "2011 Super Outbreak"), and was one of 21 EF3-rated tornadoes to be confirmed that day.[\[2\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-2)

**Quick facts** Meteorological history, Formed ...

The tornado first touched down in [Greene County](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Greene_County,_Alabama "Greene County, Alabama"), immediately producing EF2-rated damage to areas directly northwest of Tishabee. Damage was inflicted to several structures and trees as the tornado moved into the Sawyerville area, where EF3 damage was inflicted to more structures. The tornado maintained a wide and long swath of EF3 intensity at its center as it hit Eoline. The tornado would gradually weaken before lifting east of [West Blocton](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/West_Blocton,_Alabama "West Blocton, Alabama"). The tornado devastated areas in Central Alabama which it impacted; seven people were killed. The tornado had maximum estimated windspeeds of 145 miles per hour (233 km/h), classifying it as an EF3 tornado on the [Enhanced Fujita scale](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Enhanced_Fujita_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale").

### Setup

The environmental conditions leading up to the 2011 Super Outbreak were among the "most conducive to violent tornadoes ever documented".[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BAMS-3) On April 25, a vigorous upper-level [shortwave trough](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Shortwave_/(meteorology/) "Shortwave (meteorology)") moved into the Southern Plains states.[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-4) Ample instability, low-level moisture, and [wind shear](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Wind_shear "Wind shear") all fueled a significant [tornado outbreak](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tornado_outbreak "Tornado outbreak") from [Texas](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Texas "Texas") to [Tennessee](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tennessee "Tennessee"); at least 64 tornadoes touched down on this day.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BAMS-3) An [area of low pressure](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Low-pressure_area "Low-pressure area") consolidated over Texas on April 26 and traveled east while the aforementioned shortwave trough traversed the [Mississippi](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") and [Ohio River](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ohio_River "Ohio River") valleys.[\[5\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-5) Another 50 tornadoes touched down on this day.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BAMS-3) The multi-day outbreak culminated on April 27 with the most violent day of tornadic activity since the [1974 Super Outbreak](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/1974_Super_Outbreak "1974 Super Outbreak"). Multiple episodes of tornadic activity ensued with two waves of [mesoscale convective systems](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Mesoscale_convective_system "Mesoscale convective system") in the morning hours followed by a widespread outbreak of [supercells](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Supercell "Supercell") from [Mississippi](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Mississippi "Mississippi") to [North Carolina](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/North_Carolina "North Carolina") during the afternoon into the evening.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BAMS-3)

Tornadic activity on April 27 was precipitated by a 995 [mbar](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Bar_/(unit/) "Bar (unit)") ([hPa](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Pascal_/(unit/) "Pascal (unit)"); 29.39 [inHg](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Inches_of_Mercury "Inches of Mercury")) surface low situated over [Kentucky](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Kentucky "Kentucky") and a deep, negatively tilted (aligned northwest to southeast) trough over [Arkansas](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Arkansas "Arkansas") and [Louisiana](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Louisiana "Louisiana"). A strong southwesterly surface jet intersected these systems at a 60° angle, an [ageostrophic flow](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ageostrophy "Ageostrophy") that led to [storm-relative helicity](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Hydrodynamical_helicity#Meteorology "Hydrodynamical helicity") values in excess of 500 m2s−2—indicative of extreme wind shear and a very high potential for rotating [updrafts](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Vertical_draft "Vertical draft") within supercells. Ample moisture from the [Gulf of Mexico](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico") was brought north across the [Deep South](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Deep_South "Deep South"), leading to daytime high temperatures of 77 to 81 °F (25 to 27 °C) and [dewpoints](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Dewpoint "Dewpoint") of 66 to 72 °F (19 to 22 °C). Furthermore, [convective available potential energy](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Convective_available_potential_energy "Convective available potential energy") (CAPE) values reached 2,500–3,000 J/kg−1.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BAMS-3)

### Forecast

[![Image 1: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Day11630UTCOlook.gif/250px-Day11630UTCOlook.gif)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#/media/File:Day11630UTCOlook.gif)

The National Weather Service Storm Prediction Center's Day 1 Convective Outlook for April 27, showing the Categorical Graphic

[![Image 2: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Day1probotlk_20110427_tornado.png/250px-Day1probotlk_20110427_tornado.png)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#/media/File:Day1probotlk_20110427_tornado.png)

The probability of a tornado within 25 miles of a point (cross-hatched area: 10% or greater probability of EF2+ tornadoes)

On the morning of April 27, a strong [cold front](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Cold_front "Cold front") with several areas of embedded [low pressure](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Low-pressure_area "Low-pressure area") extended from the [Texas Hill Country](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Texas_Hill_Country "Texas Hill Country") northeastward towards the [Arklatex](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ark-La-Tex "Ark-La-Tex") and the [Ozarks](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ozarks "Ozarks"), and later into the lower [Ohio Valley](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ohio_River "Ohio River"). Warm moist air was in place due to strong southerly flow ahead of the front over Mississippi, Alabama, and Tennessee. An upper level disturbance sparked a broad area of [showers](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Rain "Rain") and [thunderstorms](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Thunderstorm "Thunderstorm") as it moved across the frontal boundary on the previous evening. The eastern edge of the line of showers and storms continued to move eastward, in concert with the upper disturbance, reaching the northwest Alabama border around 2:00 a.m. CDT.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:3-6)

This produced the last and most violent round of severe weather, which began around 2:30 p.m. CDT for northern Alabama as supercells began to line up to the southwest of the area. During the early afternoon hours, the potential for destructive tornadoes was highlighted by the [Storm Prediction Center](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center")'s upgrade to a [high risk](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Storm_Prediction_Center_high_risk_days "List of Storm Prediction Center high risk days") for severe weather around 1:00 p.m. CDT.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:3-6) This prompted a [particularly dangerous situation](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Particularly_dangerous_situation "Particularly dangerous situation") (PDS) [tornado watch](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tornado_watch "Tornado watch"), which was issued for northern Alabama and portions of southern [Tennessee](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tennessee "Tennessee") at 1:45 p.m. CDT. The bulletin that accompanied the watch read:[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-7)

> THE NWS STORM PREDICTION CENTER HAS ISSUED A TORNADO WATCH FOR PORTIONS OF: MUCH OF ALABAMA, NORTHWEST GEORGIA, SOUTHEAST MISSISSIPPI, SOUTHERN MIDDLE TENNESSEE, EFFECTIVE THIS WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON AND EVENING FROM 145 PM UNTIL 1000 PM CDT.
> 
> ...THIS IS A PARTICULARLY DANGEROUS SITUATION...
> 
> DESTRUCTIVE TORNADOES...LARGE HAIL TO 4 INCHES IN DIAMETER. THUNDERSTORM WIND GUSTS TO 80 MPH...AND DANGEROUS LIGHTNING ARE POSSIBLE IN THESE AREAS.

The potential for tornadoes ramped up from noon through 9:00 p.m. CDT. During this period, much of Alabama experienced numerous [supercell thunderstorms](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Supercell "Supercell") that produced numerous tornadoes, including the Sawyerville tornado.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:3-6)[\[8\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-9)

[![Image 3: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Deroofed_building_near_Tishabee%2C_Alabama_-_April_27%2C_2011.jpg/640px-Deroofed_building_near_Tishabee%2C_Alabama_-_April_27%2C_2011.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#/media/File:Deroofed_building_near_Tishabee,_Alabama_-_April_27,_2011.jpg)

A deroofed building near Tishabee

The tornado first touched down near Head Drive and County Road 69 in extreme southwest [Greene County](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Greene_County,_Alabama "Greene County, Alabama") to the west-southwest of [Tishabee](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tishabee,_Alabama "Tishabee, Alabama"), near the [Sumter County](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Sumter_County,_Alabama "Sumter County, Alabama") border, at 5:30 p.m. CDT (22:30 UTC). EF1-rated damage was immediately inflicted to mobile homes along County Road 69, and a barn received damage near December Lane. The tornado reached EF2 intensity as it crossed County Road 79, where it damaged a barn, destroyed two small churches, and damaged at least four mobile homes. Further EF1 damage was inflicted to softwood trees near the intersection of County Road 69 and County Road 70. The tornado continued to impact areas just north of Tishabee before crossing County Road 72 at EF2 intensity. Further northeast, the tornado passed over Reed Lake and the Acron Creek, before impacting County Road 50. It then crossed the McConnico Creek, moving northeast and hitting County Road 49.[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:0-10)[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[11\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-11)

EF2 damage was inflicted to several double-wide mobile homes as the tornado moved over County Road 48. After impacting County Road 20, the tornado inflicted EF2 damage to a metal outbuilding, sheering steel beams off its concrete foundation and removing both the walls and roof from the structure. While crossing [U.S. 43](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/U.S._Route_43 "U.S. Route 43"), the tornado continued to cause substantial roof and wall damage to several brick buildings and homes. Hundreds of trees were downed in this area as well. More EF2 damage was inflicted to a metal building system south of the Dollarhide Creek, and a building suffered an exterior wall collapse nearby. Windspeeds in this area were estimated by the [National Weather Service](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") office in [Birmingham, Alabama](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama") (NWS BMX) to have been as high as 135 miles per hour (217 km/h).[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:0-10) Two people sustained minor injuries in Greene County as the tornado continued along a primarily rural path northeast, moving across the [Black Warrior River](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Black_Warrior_River "Black Warrior River") and into [Hale County](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Hale_County,_Alabama "Hale County, Alabama").[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[12\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-GreeneCo_NCDC-12)

### Track near Sawyerville and Hale County

[![Image 4: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/EF3_damage_to_a_brick_home_near_Sawyerville%2C_Alabama.jpg/640px-EF3_damage_to_a_brick_home_near_Sawyerville%2C_Alabama.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#/media/File:EF3_damage_to_a_brick_home_near_Sawyerville,_Alabama.jpg)

EF3-rated damage to a brick home near Sawyerville

The tornado entered Hale County along the Wrights Creek located west of Sawyerville, continuing to move through sparsely-populated rural areas. The tornado crossed Erie Road at EF2 intensity and the intersection of County Road 92 and Erie Road to the north, nearing areas directly north of Sawyerville. It impacted the Lawson Lakes and moved over the Wrights Creek a second time, and to the northeast crossed over Coleman Road and [Alabama State Highway 14](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Alabama_State_Route_14 "Alabama State Route 14"). The northern portion of Webb Lane was also struck by the outer portions of the tornado. It first reached EF3 intensity east of County Road 17, inflicting heavy damage to a mobile home along County Road 18. Softwood trees were snapped at EF2 intensity on the western portions of the road prior to the tornado reaching EF3 intensity. A brick home, also located on County Road 18, sustained heavy damage, with all walls of the home collapsing in the tornadic winds. Several more mobile homes received EF3-rated damage nearby before the tornado crossed over County Road 30.[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:0-10) The tornado weakened to EF2 intensity north of Tree Top Road, before restrengthening along County Road 21 and the Calwell Creek area. Several brick homes were completely destroyed at EF3 intensity, and EF1 to EF2 damage was inflicted to homes south of County Road 32. It retained EF3-level strength as it tracked northeast on Dunson Road, before bending steel poles on Raspberry Road. As this point in its track, the tornado was moving through rural areas south and east of the small communities of Harper Hill and Ingram. On Hubbard Road, a mobile home was completely destroyed at EF3 intensity and softwood trees were snapped on the southern edge of the tornado's path. EF1 damage was inflicted to homes and hardwood trees as the tornado crossed County Road 31, before the tornado began moving parallel to the Fivemile Creek. The tornado moved across the northern portions of Strawberry Road as it moved northeast, before passing a short distance south of Ingram. On County Road 29, the tornado impacted a wood-framed church and twisted the undercarriage of at least one mobile home. The tornado then moved over Hoggle Road, before impacting the Latner Branch Creek. The tornado maintained EF3 intensity as it crossed Clary Hill Road and then over the southern portions of NF Road 708, continuing to move northeast. EF2-rated damage was inflicted to pine trees on County Road 49 north of the Payne Lake.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:0-10)[\[13\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-HaleCoEF3_NCDC-13) A wedding photo in Sawyerville set aloft by the tornado was found across the state in [St. Clair County](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/St._Clair_County,_Alabama "St. Clair County, Alabama").[\[14\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-14)

### Damage in Eoline

[![Image 5: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Damaged_home_near_Water_Oak%2C_Alabama_-_April_27%2C_2011.jpg/640px-Damaged_home_near_Water_Oak%2C_Alabama_-_April_27%2C_2011.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#/media/File:Damaged_home_near_Water_Oak,_Alabama_-_April_27,_2011.jpg)

Damaged home near Water Oak

Leaving behind six fatalities and forty more injuries, the tornado maintained its intensity as it moved into the [Talladega National Forest](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Talladega_National_Forest "Talladega National Forest"). It downed a significant number of trees before moving into [Bibb County](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Bibb_County,_Alabama "Bibb County, Alabama") north of [Alabama State Highway 25](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Alabama_State_Route_25 "Alabama State Route 25").[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[13\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-HaleCoEF3_NCDC-13) The tornado moved over Road 718 in extreme western Bibb County before crossing Road 727 north of Mertz. It impacted Caddis Road in the National Forest, maintaining EF3 intensity at its center. The tornado moved along West Eoline Road as it neared the communities of [Eoline](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Eoline,_Alabama "Eoline, Alabama"), Pleasant Hill, Ingate and Choctaw Hills. EF3-rated damage was inflicted to mobile homes along Murphy Road as the tornado moved into the southern portions of Eoline. On Mooney Creek Lane, the tornado destroyed the Eoline Volunteer Fire Department and damaged the vinyl siding of numerous homes;[\[15\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-16) a tree fell on one property. Twelve people survived the tornado by taking shelter in the station's hallway.[\[17\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-17) Additional EF3 damage was inflicted to hardwood trees, which were uprooted and snapped inside wind speeds that were estimated to have been as high as 125 miles per hour (201 km/h). In Eoline alone, around one dozen mobile homes and single-family site-built homes were destroyed, while many more sustained anywhere from minor to major damage.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:0-10)

One person was killed in Eoline, in a vehicle near the destroyed fire department. Ten others were injured before the tornado crossed [U.S. Highway 82](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/U.S._Route_82 "U.S. Route 82") at EF3 intensity, shifting an entire home off its foundation along the highway. To the north, large hardwood trees were uprooted on Eoline Road. The tornado weakened as it crossed Countryside Road, although it still retained EF2-equivalent strength. It then moved south of Scottsvile, which was directly impacted by an EF1-rated tornado on April 15, during a [separate tornado outbreak](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tornado_outbreak_of_April_14%E2%80%9316,_2011 "Tornado outbreak of April 14–16, 2011") earlier in the month.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:0-10)[\[18\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BibbCoEF3_NCDC-18)

[![Image 6: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/EolineFireDept.jpg/640px-EolineFireDept.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#/media/File:EolineFireDept.jpg)

Heavy damage to the Eoline Volunteer Fire Department

Northeast of Eoline, the tornado weakened to EF2 intensity, continuing to cause significant damage as it crossed County Road 9, [Alabama State Highway 5](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Alabama_State_Route_5 "Alabama State Route 5"), and County Road 26, south of [West Blocton](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/West_Blocton,_Alabama "West Blocton, Alabama"). Several mobile homes and site-built homes were either destroyed or sustained major damage. Along the path, thousands of trees were downed. The tornado continued to weaken as it moved to the east of West Blocton, continuing to knock down trees. More trees were downed as the tornado crossed the [Cahaba River](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Cahaba_River "Cahaba River") and lifted just northeast of [Marvel](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Marvel,_Alabama "Marvel, Alabama") at 6:55 p.m. CDT (23:55 UTC), not far from the [Shelby County](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Shelby_County,_Alabama "Shelby County, Alabama") border.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[18\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BibbCoEF3_NCDC-18)

The tornado was rated as an EF3, with maximum sustained winds of 145 mph (233 km/h). It remained on the ground for almost an hour and a half, traversing 72.13 miles (116.08 km), being, at times, about one mile (1.6 km) wide. In total, seven people were killed and at least 52 others were injured.[\[1\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[12\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-GreeneCo_NCDC-12)[\[13\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-HaleCoEF3_NCDC-13)[\[18\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BibbCoEF3_NCDC-18) The storm that produced the Sawyerville EF3 later produced an EF0 tornado east of [Pell City, Alabama](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Pell_City,_Alabama "Pell City, Alabama").[\[19\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-19)

### Damage, recovery efforts and studies

Immediately following the tornado, the Greensboro Recreational Center in [Greensboro, Alabama](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Greensboro,_Alabama "Greensboro, Alabama") provided food, clothing and other household items for victims of the tornado.[\[20\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-20) The annual "Spring Ding-a-Ling-Dong" helped raise money that went towards the relief efforts in Sawyerville.[\[21\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-21)

The tornado was rated as an EF3, with maximum sustained winds of 145 mph (233 km/h). It remained on the ground for almost an hour and a half, traversing 72.13 miles (116.08 km), being, at times, about one mile (1.6 km) wide.[\[22\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-22) Approximately 30% of the tornado's path consisted of EF0-rated damage indicators (DIs), 25% contained EF1-rated DIs, 28% contained EF2-rated DIs and 7% contained EF3-rated DIs on the [Damage Assessment Toolkit](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Damage_Assessment_Toolkit "Damage Assessment Toolkit").[\[23\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-23) A May 2014 study by researchers at the [Florida State University](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Florida_State_University "Florida State University") found that the tornado had a kinetic energy level of 123 [terajoules](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Terajoule "Terajoule"), twice as much as the amount of kinetic energy that was released during the 1945 [nuclear bombing of Hiroshima, Japan](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Bombing_of_Hiroshima "Bombing of Hiroshima"). The kinetic energy was the highest observed in the study, above the levels of the [Hackleburg–Phil Campbell EF5 tornado](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Hackleburg%E2%80%93Phil_Campbell_tornado "2011 Hackleburg–Phil Campbell tornado"), [Shoal Creek Valley–Ohatchee EF4 tornado](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Shoal_Creek_Valley%E2%80%93Ohatchee_tornado "2011 Shoal Creek Valley–Ohatchee tornado"), [Smithville EF5 tornado](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Smithville_tornado "2011 Smithville tornado") from the same day, and the [2013 Moore, Oklahoma EF5 tornado](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2013_Moore_tornado "2013 Moore tornado").[\[24\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-24)

In 2024, four new storm shelters were scheduled to be constructed in Hale County. The county's Emergency Management Agency Director Russell Weeden stated that "I feel like those injuries and fatalities could have been prevented if we had a safe place for them to go," in relation to the 2011 tornado and separate tornadoes that hit the county in 2023.[\[25\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:2-25) The shelters were planned to have been open in October 2024.[\[25\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:2-25)

### Casualties

Seven people were killed by the tornado; six in Hale County and one in Bibb County:[\[26\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-26)

Click here for more information.") From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
2011 Sawyerville–Eoline tornado

The tornado, seen as it was at EF2 or EF3 intensity near Forkland, Alabama

Meteorological history
FormedApril 27, 2011, 5:30 p.m. CDT (UTC−05:00)
DissipatedApril 27, 2011, 6:55 p.m. CDT (UTC−05:00)
Duration1 hour, 25 minutes
EF3 tornado
on the Enhanced Fujita scale
Highest winds145 mph (233 km/h)
Overall effects
Fatalities7
Injuries52
Part of the 2011 Super Outbreak and Tornadoes of 2011
On the afternoon of April 27, 2011, a large, long-tracked, and destructive low-end EF3 tornado, known as the **Sawyerville–Eoline tornado**,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1) moved across [Central Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Alabama "Central Alabama"), in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), moving through areas near numerous towns along its 72.1-mile (116.0 km) track, including [Tishabee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tishabee,_Alabama "Tishabee, Alabama"), [Sawyerville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sawyerville,_Alabama "Sawyerville, Alabama"), [Havana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana,_Alabama "Havana, Alabama") and [Eoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eoline,_Alabama "Eoline, Alabama"). The tornado killed seven, injured 52, and impacted hundreds of structures. It occurred as part of the [largest tornado outbreak in modern history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak "2011 Super Outbreak"), and was one of 21 EF3-rated tornadoes to be confirmed that day.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-2) The tornado first touched down in [Greene County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greene_County,_Alabama "Greene County, Alabama"), immediately producing EF2-rated damage to areas directly northwest of Tishabee. Damage was inflicted to several structures and trees as the tornado moved into the Sawyerville area, where EF3 damage was inflicted to more structures. The tornado maintained a wide and long swath of EF3 intensity at its center as it hit Eoline. The tornado would gradually weaken before lifting east of [West Blocton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Blocton,_Alabama "West Blocton, Alabama"). The tornado devastated areas in Central Alabama which it impacted; seven people were killed. The tornado had maximum estimated windspeeds of 145 miles per hour (233 km/h), classifying it as an EF3 tornado on the [Enhanced Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_Fujita_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale"). Meteorological synopsis ----------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Meteorological synopsis")\] The environmental conditions leading up to the 2011 Super Outbreak were among the "most conducive to violent tornadoes ever documented".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BAMS-3) On April 25, a vigorous upper-level [shortwave trough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortwave_/(meteorology/) "Shortwave (meteorology)") moved into the Southern Plains states.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-4) Ample instability, low-level moisture, and [wind shear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_shear "Wind shear") all fueled a significant [tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak "Tornado outbreak") from [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") to [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"); at least 64 tornadoes touched down on this day.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BAMS-3) An [area of low pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-pressure_area "Low-pressure area") consolidated over Texas on April 26 and traveled east while the aforementioned shortwave trough traversed the [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") and [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") valleys.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-5) Another 50 tornadoes touched down on this day.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BAMS-3) The multi-day outbreak culminated on April 27 with the most violent day of tornadic activity since the [1974 Super Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Super_Outbreak "1974 Super Outbreak"). Multiple episodes of tornadic activity ensued with two waves of [mesoscale convective systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoscale_convective_system "Mesoscale convective system") in the morning hours followed by a widespread outbreak of [supercells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") from [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi") to [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina") during the afternoon into the evening.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BAMS-3) Tornadic activity on April 27 was precipitated by a 995 [mbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_/(unit/) "Bar (unit)") ([hPa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_/(unit/) "Pascal (unit)"); 29.39 [inHg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inches_of_Mercury "Inches of Mercury")) surface low situated over [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky") and a deep, negatively tilted (aligned northwest to southeast) trough over [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas") and [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"). A strong southwesterly surface jet intersected these systems at a 60° angle, an [ageostrophic flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ageostrophy "Ageostrophy") that led to [storm-relative helicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrodynamical_helicity#Meteorology "Hydrodynamical helicity") values in excess of 500 m2s−2—indicative of extreme wind shear and a very high potential for rotating [updrafts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_draft "Vertical draft") within supercells. Ample moisture from the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico") was brought north across the [Deep South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_South "Deep South"), leading to daytime high temperatures of 77 to 81 °F (25 to 27 °C) and [dewpoints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewpoint "Dewpoint") of 66 to 72 °F (19 to 22 °C). Furthermore, [convective available potential energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convective_available_potential_energy "Convective available potential energy") (CAPE) values reached 2,500–3,000 J/kg−1.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BAMS-3) [![Image 3: The National Weather Service Storm Prediction Center outlined a high risk area for severe weather over central Alabama on this map.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Day11630UTCOlook.gif/250px-Day11630UTCOlook.gif)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Day11630UTCOlook.gif) The National Weather Service Storm Prediction Center's Day 1 Convective Outlook for April 27, showing the Categorical Graphic [![Image 4: This version of the map shows a 45% probability of a tornado within 25 miles of a given point in the highest risk area, and a 10% chance of a significant tornado.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Day1probotlk_20110427_tornado.png/250px-Day1probotlk_20110427_tornado.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Day1probotlk_20110427_tornado.png) The probability of a tornado within 25 miles of a point (cross-hatched area: 10% or greater probability of EF2+ tornadoes) On the morning of April 27, a strong [cold front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_front "Cold front") with several areas of embedded [low pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-pressure_area "Low-pressure area") extended from the [Texas Hill Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Hill_Country "Texas Hill Country") northeastward towards the [Arklatex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ark-La-Tex "Ark-La-Tex") and the [Ozarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozarks "Ozarks"), and later into the lower [Ohio Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River"). Warm moist air was in place due to strong southerly flow ahead of the front over Mississippi, Alabama, and Tennessee. An upper level disturbance sparked a broad area of [showers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain "Rain") and [thunderstorms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunderstorm "Thunderstorm") as it moved across the frontal boundary on the previous evening. The eastern edge of the line of showers and storms continued to move eastward, in concert with the upper disturbance, reaching the northwest Alabama border around 2:00 a.m. CDT.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:3-6) This produced the last and most violent round of severe weather, which began around 2:30 p.m. CDT for northern Alabama as supercells began to line up to the southwest of the area. During the early afternoon hours, the potential for destructive tornadoes was highlighted by the [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center")'s upgrade to a [high risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Storm_Prediction_Center_high_risk_days "List of Storm Prediction Center high risk days") for severe weather around 1:00 p.m. CDT.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:3-6) This prompted a [particularly dangerous situation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particularly_dangerous_situation "Particularly dangerous situation") (PDS) [tornado watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_watch "Tornado watch"), which was issued for northern Alabama and portions of southern [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee") at 1:45 p.m. CDT. The bulletin that accompanied the watch read:[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-7) > THE NWS STORM PREDICTION CENTER HAS ISSUED A TORNADO WATCH FOR PORTIONS OF: MUCH OF ALABAMA, NORTHWEST GEORGIA, SOUTHEAST MISSISSIPPI, SOUTHERN MIDDLE TENNESSEE, EFFECTIVE THIS WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON AND EVENING FROM 145 PM UNTIL 1000 PM CDT. > > ...THIS IS A PARTICULARLY DANGEROUS SITUATION... > > DESTRUCTIVE TORNADOES...LARGE HAIL TO 4 INCHES IN DIAMETER. THUNDERSTORM WIND GUSTS TO 80 MPH...AND DANGEROUS LIGHTNING ARE POSSIBLE IN THESE AREAS. The potential for tornadoes ramped up from noon through 9:00 p.m. CDT. During this period, much of Alabama experienced numerous [supercell thunderstorms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") that produced numerous tornadoes, including the Sawyerville tornado.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:3-6)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-9) [![Image 5: A brick building with it's roof removed. Trees can be seen in the background. On the bottom left, it says "NWS BMX".](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Deroofed_building_near_Tishabee%2C_Alabama_-_April_27%2C_2011.jpg/250px-Deroofed_building_near_Tishabee%2C_Alabama_-_April_27%2C_2011.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Deroofed_building_near_Tishabee,_Alabama_-_April_27,_2011.jpg) A deroofed building near Tishabee The tornado first touched down near Head Drive and County Road 69 in extreme southwest [Greene County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greene_County,_Alabama "Greene County, Alabama") to the west-southwest of [Tishabee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tishabee,_Alabama "Tishabee, Alabama"), near the [Sumter County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumter_County,_Alabama "Sumter County, Alabama") border, at 5:30 p.m. CDT (22:30 UTC). EF1-rated damage was immediately inflicted to mobile homes along County Road 69, and a barn received damage near December Lane. The tornado reached EF2 intensity as it crossed County Road 79, where it damaged a barn, destroyed two small churches, and damaged at least four mobile homes. Further EF1 damage was inflicted to softwood trees near the intersection of County Road 69 and County Road 70. The tornado continued to impact areas just north of Tishabee before crossing County Road 72 at EF2 intensity. Further northeast, the tornado passed over Reed Lake and the Acron Creek, before impacting County Road 50. It then crossed the McConnico Creek, moving northeast and hitting County Road 49.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:0-10)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-11) EF2 damage was inflicted to several double-wide mobile homes as the tornado moved over County Road 48. After impacting County Road 20, the tornado inflicted EF2 damage to a metal outbuilding, sheering steel beams off its concrete foundation and removing both the walls and roof from the structure. While crossing [U.S. 43](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_43 "U.S. Route 43"), the tornado continued to cause substantial roof and wall damage to several brick buildings and homes. Hundreds of trees were downed in this area as well. More EF2 damage was inflicted to a metal building system south of the Dollarhide Creek, and a building suffered an exterior wall collapse nearby. Windspeeds in this area were estimated by the [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") office in [Birmingham, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama") (NWS BMX) to have been as high as 135 miles per hour (217 km/h).[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:0-10) Two people sustained minor injuries in Greene County as the tornado continued along a primarily rural path northeast, moving across the [Black Warrior River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Warrior_River "Black Warrior River") and into [Hale County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hale_County,_Alabama "Hale County, Alabama").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-GreeneCo_NCDC-12) ### Track near Sawyerville and Hale County \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Track near Sawyerville and Hale County")\] [![Image 6: A red brick home surrounded by grass, seen destroyed. A debarked tree stands to its left.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/EF3_damage_to_a_brick_home_near_Sawyerville%2C_Alabama.jpg/250px-EF3_damage_to_a_brick_home_near_Sawyerville%2C_Alabama.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EF3_damage_to_a_brick_home_near_Sawyerville,_Alabama.jpg) EF3-rated damage to a brick home near Sawyerville The tornado entered Hale County along the Wrights Creek located west of Sawyerville, continuing to move through sparsely-populated rural areas. The tornado crossed Erie Road at EF2 intensity and the intersection of County Road 92 and Erie Road to the north, nearing areas directly north of Sawyerville. It impacted the Lawson Lakes and moved over the Wrights Creek a second time, and to the northeast crossed over Coleman Road and [Alabama State Highway 14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_State_Route_14 "Alabama State Route 14"). The northern portion of Webb Lane was also struck by the outer portions of the tornado. It first reached EF3 intensity east of County Road 17, inflicting heavy damage to a mobile home along County Road 18. Softwood trees were snapped at EF2 intensity on the western portions of the road prior to the tornado reaching EF3 intensity. A brick home, also located on County Road 18, sustained heavy damage, with all walls of the home collapsing in the tornadic winds. Several more mobile homes received EF3-rated damage nearby before the tornado crossed over County Road 30.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:0-10) The tornado weakened to EF2 intensity north of Tree Top Road, before restrengthening along County Road 21 and the Calwell Creek area. Several brick homes were completely destroyed at EF3 intensity, and EF1 to EF2 damage was inflicted to homes south of County Road 32. It retained EF3-level strength as it tracked northeast on Dunson Road, before bending steel poles on Raspberry Road. As this point in its track, the tornado was moving through rural areas south and east of the small communities of [Harper Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harper_Hill,_Alabama&action=edit&redlink=1 "Harper Hill, Alabama (page does not exist)") and [Ingram](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ingram,_Alabama&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ingram, Alabama (page does not exist)"). On Hubbard Road, a mobile home was completely destroyed at EF3 intensity and softwood trees were snapped on the southern edge of the tornado's path. EF1 damage was inflicted to homes and hardwood trees as the tornado crossed County Road 31, before the tornado began moving parallel to the Fivemile Creek. The tornado moved across the northern portions of Strawberry Road as it moved northeast, before passing a short distance south of Ingram. On County Road 29, the tornado impacted a wood-framed church and twisted the undercarriage of at least one mobile home. The tornado then moved over Hoggle Road, before impacting the Latner Branch Creek. The tornado maintained EF3 intensity as it crossed Clary Hill Road and then over the southern portions of NF Road 708, continuing to move northeast. EF2-rated damage was inflicted to pine trees on County Road 49 north of the Payne Lake.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:0-10)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-HaleCoEF3_NCDC-13) A wedding photo in Sawyerville set aloft by the tornado was found across the state in [St. Clair County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Clair_County,_Alabama "St. Clair County, Alabama").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-14) [![Image 7: A ravine or pit filled with tree debris and multiple white cars. On the bottom left, it says "NWS BMX".](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Damaged_home_near_Water_Oak%2C_Alabama_-_April_27%2C_2011.jpg/250px-Damaged_home_near_Water_Oak%2C_Alabama_-_April_27%2C_2011.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Damaged_home_near_Water_Oak,_Alabama_-_April_27,_2011.jpg) Damaged home near Water Oak Leaving behind six fatalities and forty more injuries, the tornado maintained its intensity as it moved into the [Talladega National Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talladega_National_Forest "Talladega National Forest"). It downed a significant number of trees before moving into [Bibb County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibb_County,_Alabama "Bibb County, Alabama") north of [Alabama State Highway 25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_State_Route_25 "Alabama State Route 25").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-HaleCoEF3_NCDC-13) The tornado moved over Road 718 in extreme western Bibb County before crossing Road 727 north of Mertz. It impacted Caddis Road in the National Forest, maintaining EF3 intensity at its center. The tornado moved along West Eoline Road as it neared the communities of [Eoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eoline,_Alabama "Eoline, Alabama"), Pleasant Hill, Ingate and Choctaw Hills. EF3-rated damage was inflicted to mobile homes along Murphy Road as the tornado moved into the southern portions of Eoline. On Mooney Creek Lane, the tornado destroyed the Eoline Volunteer Fire Department and damaged the vinyl siding of numerous homes;[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-16) a tree fell on one property. Twelve people survived the tornado by taking shelter in the station's hallway.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-17) Additional EF3 damage was inflicted to hardwood trees, which were uprooted and snapped inside wind speeds that were estimated to have been as high as 125 miles per hour (201 km/h). In Eoline alone, around one dozen mobile homes and single-family site-built homes were destroyed, while many more sustained anywhere from minor to major damage.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:0-10) One person was killed in Eoline, in a vehicle near the destroyed fire department. Ten others were injured before the tornado crossed [U.S. Highway 82](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_82 "U.S. Route 82") at EF3 intensity, shifting an entire home off its foundation along the highway. To the north, large hardwood trees were uprooted on Eoline Road. The tornado weakened as it crossed Countryside Road, although it still retained EF2-equivalent strength. It then moved south of Scottsvile, which was directly impacted by an EF1-rated tornado on April 15, during a [separate tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_April_14%E2%80%9316,_2011 "Tornado outbreak of April 14–16, 2011") earlier in the month.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:0-10)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BibbCoEF3_NCDC-18) [![Image 8: A building completely destroyed with trees in the background. Two cars are visible, one of which looks slightly damaged. On the bottom left, it says "NWS BMX".](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/EolineFireDept.jpg/250px-EolineFireDept.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EolineFireDept.jpg) Heavy damage to the Eoline Volunteer Fire Department Northeast of Eoline, the tornado weakened to EF2 intensity, continuing to cause significant damage as it crossed County Road 9, [Alabama State Highway 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_State_Route_5 "Alabama State Route 5"), and County Road 26, south of [West Blocton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Blocton,_Alabama "West Blocton, Alabama"). Several mobile homes and site-built homes were either destroyed or sustained major damage. Along the path, thousands of trees were downed. The tornado continued to weaken as it moved to the east of West Blocton, continuing to knock down trees. More trees were downed as the tornado crossed the [Cahaba River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahaba_River "Cahaba River") and lifted just northeast of [Marvel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel,_Alabama "Marvel, Alabama") at 6:55 p.m. CDT (23:55 UTC), not far from the [Shelby County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelby_County,_Alabama "Shelby County, Alabama") border.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BibbCoEF3_NCDC-18) The tornado was rated as an EF3, with maximum sustained winds of 145 mph (233 km/h). It remained on the ground for almost an hour and a half, traversing 72.13 miles (116.08 km), being, at times, about one mile (1.6 km) wide. In total, seven people were killed and at least 52 others were injured.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-Sawyerville/Eoline_tornado-1)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-GreeneCo_NCDC-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-HaleCoEF3_NCDC-13)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-BibbCoEF3_NCDC-18) The storm that produced the Sawyerville EF3 later produced an EF0 tornado east of [Pell City, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell_City,_Alabama "Pell City, Alabama").[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-19) ### Damage, recovery efforts and studies \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Damage, recovery efforts and studies")\] Immediately following the tornado, the Greensboro Recreational Center in [Greensboro, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensboro,_Alabama "Greensboro, Alabama") provided food, clothing and other household items for victims of the tornado.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-20) The annual "Spring Ding-a-Ling-Dong" helped raise money that went towards the relief efforts in Sawyerville.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-21) The tornado was rated as an EF3, with maximum sustained winds of 145 mph (233 km/h). It remained on the ground for almost an hour and a half, traversing 72.13 miles (116.08 km), being, at times, about one mile (1.6 km) wide.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-22) Approximately 30% of the tornado's path consisted of EF0-rated damage indicators (DIs), 25% contained EF1-rated DIs, 28% contained EF2-rated DIs and 7% contained EF3-rated DIs on the [Damage Assessment Toolkit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damage_Assessment_Toolkit "Damage Assessment Toolkit").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-23) A May 2014 study by researchers at the [Florida State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_State_University "Florida State University") found that the tornado had a kinetic energy level of 123 [terajoules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terajoule "Terajoule"), twice as much as the amount of kinetic energy that was released during the 1945 [nuclear bombing of Hiroshima, Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Hiroshima "Bombing of Hiroshima"). The kinetic energy was the highest observed in the study, above the levels of the [Hackleburg–Phil Campbell EF5 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Hackleburg%E2%80%93Phil_Campbell_tornado "2011 Hackleburg–Phil Campbell tornado"), [Shoal Creek Valley–Ohatchee EF4 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Shoal_Creek_Valley%E2%80%93Ohatchee_tornado "2011 Shoal Creek Valley–Ohatchee tornado"), [Smithville EF5 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Smithville_tornado "2011 Smithville tornado") from the same day, and the [2013 Moore, Oklahoma EF5 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Moore_tornado "2013 Moore tornado").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-24) In 2024, four new storm shelters were scheduled to be constructed in Hale County. The county's Emergency Management Agency Director Russell Weeden stated that "I feel like those injuries and fatalities could have been prevented if we had a safe place for them to go," in relation to the 2011 tornado and separate tornadoes that hit the county in 2023.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:2-25) The shelters were planned to have been open in October 2024.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-:2-25) Seven people were killed by the tornado; six in Hale County and one in Bibb County:[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Sawyerville%E2%80%93Eoline_tornado#cite_note-26)

Summary map from the April 25-28, 2011 Super Outbreak via U.S. Tornadoes.

362 Confirmed Tornadoes

4 Rated EF5.  11 Rated EF4.  21 Rated EF3.

207 Tornadoes on April 27.  Most ever in a 24-hour period.

324 Fatalities.  Over 3100 Injuries.

Estimated $12 Billion In Damage.

“The individual tornado paths from the April 25-28, 2011, Super Outbreak added up to an almost unfathomable 3,200 path miles, by far the greatest of any U.S. outbreak. This total path was over 600 miles longer than the April 3-4, 1974, Super Outbreak.” – Dr. Greg Forbes

The 2011 Super Outbreak was the largest and costliest[note 1] tornado outbreak ever recorded, taking place in the Southern, Midwestern, and Northeastern United States from April 25 to 28, 2011, leaving catastrophic destruction in its wake.[9][10][11][12] Over 175 tornadoes struck Alabama, Mississippi, and Tennessee, which were the most severely damaged states. Other destructive tornadoes occurred in Arkansas, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, New York, and Virginia, with storms also affecting other states in the Southern and Eastern United States. In total, 368 tornadoes were confirmed by NOAA's National Weather Service (NWS) and Government of Canada's Environment Canada in 21 states from Texas to New York to southern Canada. Widespread and destructive tornadoes occurred on each day of the outbreak. April 27 was the most active day, with a record 224 tornadoes touching down that day from midnight to midnight CDT (05:00–05:00 UTC). Four of the tornadoes were rated EF5, which is the highest ranking on the Enhanced Fujita scale; typically these tornadoes are recorded no more than once a year.[11]
In total, 348 people were killed as a result of the outbreak, including 324 tornado-related deaths across six states and 24 fatalities caused by other thunderstorm-related events such as straight-line winds, hail, flash flooding or lightning.[13][14] In Alabama alone, 238 tornado-related deaths were confirmed by the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) and the state's Emergency Management Agency.[3][13] April 27's 316 fatalities were the most tornado-related fatalities in the United States in a single day since the "Tri-State" outbreak on March 18, 1925 (when at least 751 people were killed).[15][16][17][18] Nearly 500 preliminary local storm reports were received for tornadoes over four days, including 292 in 16 states on April 27 alone.[19] This event was the costliest tornado outbreak in United States history, with total damage reaching $10.2 billion (equivalent to $14 billion in 2024).[20] In 2023, tornado expert Thomas P. Grazulis created the outbreak intensity score (OIS) as a way to rank various tornado outbreaks. The 2011 Super Outbreak received an OIS of 383, making it the second most intense tornado outbreak in recorded history behind only the 1974 Super Outbreak.[21]

The outbreak was caused by a vigorous upper-level trough that moved into the Southern Plains states on April 25. An extratropical cyclone developed ahead of this upper-level trough between northeastern Oklahoma and western Missouri, and moved northeastward.[22] Conditions were similar on April 26, with a predicted likelihood of severe thunderstorms, including an extended threat of strong to violent long-track tornadoes throughout the afternoon and evening; mixed-layer CAPE values were forecast to be around 3000–4000 J/kg, around east Texas, Louisiana, and Arkansas. The storm mode on April 26 was predicted to include mostly discrete tornadic supercells during both the afternoon and the early evening, shifting over to a mesoscale convective complex, with more of a threat of damaging winds and hail during the nighttime.[23]
As the storm system moved eastward toward the Ohio, Mississippi, and Tennessee Valleys on April 27, a very powerful 80–100 knot mid-level jet stream moved into the Ohio and Tennessee Valleys behind the trough and created strong wind shear, along with a low pressure center moving quickly northeastward across those areas on April 27. During the afternoon of April 27, CAPE values were estimated to be in the range of 2000–3000 J/kg across Louisiana and southern Mississippi, with the moderate instability moving northeastward across the southern Tennessee Valley; additionally, temperatures across the southeastern United States ranged from the 70s °F (mid-20s °C) to the lower 90s °F (near 35 °C). Helicity levels ranged from 450 to 600 m2/s2, which supported some significant tornadic activity and strong to violent long-track tornadoes.[24]
A total of 56 severe weather watches were issued by the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) over those four days in the outbreak area. This included 41 tornado watches—10 of which were particularly dangerous situation (PDS) watches—and 15 severe thunderstorm watches.[25][26] The SPC assigns numbers to each severe weather watch issued starting at the beginning of each year; the organization unsuccessfully used two of their allocated watch numbers during this outbreak (numbers 208 and 209).[27][clarification needed]

April 25[edit]
A large area of possible severe storms for April 25–27 was forecast as the Storm Prediction Center (SPC) issued a moderate risk of severe weather for three consecutive days, centered over Arkansas through Tennessee. At 3:25 p.m. CDT (20:25 UTC), the SPC issued a particularly dangerous situation (PDS) tornado watch for much of Arkansas and parts of Missouri, Oklahoma, Texas, and Louisiana.[28]  By the evening of April 25, tornadoes had been reported across a few states, some of which caused significant damage in Arkansas. An intense supercell thunderstorm tracked near the Little Rock area and a tornado emergency was declared for the city of Vilonia. A large EF2 wedge tornado struck the town, subsequently causing severe damage and killing four people.[29][30] A strong EF3 tornado also struck the Hot Springs Village area earlier that evening; the tornado caused severe damage and resulted in one death. Later that evening, another EF2 tornado caused extensive damage to both a school building and Little Rock Air Force Base as well.[31] Severe flooding continued across a large area from the Red River valley to the Great Lakes.[32] A total of 42 tornadoes and five tornado-related deaths were confirmed on the 25th.

April 26[edit]
This animation of satellite images from April 26 through the morning of April 28 shows the development of the storm system which spawned the tornadoes.
A high risk of severe weather was issued for April 26 for portions of Louisiana, Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Texas along and near the Interstate 30 corridor as conditions became even more favorable for extreme weather.[33] A large PDS tornado watch with very high possibilities for tornadoes was issued for that same area that afternoon.[34] Widespread tornado warnings were then issued in that area later that evening.[35][36][37]
An upper-level negatively tilted trough with two embedded shortwaves generated two surface lows that propagated generally east. One of the surface lows tracked northeast along the Mississippi River into Wisconsin as it occluded. Tornado watches were issued for the Lower Great Lakes during the afternoon as supercell thunderstorms developed along the warm front lifting north across central Michigan. Two tornadoes touched down in Michigan and caused damage to farm structures. Further east, severe thunderstorms caused scattered wind damage and large hail across Pennsylvania and New York. Two-inch-diameter hail was reported in Lock Haven, Pennsylvania.[38] An isolated supercell moved across Central New York throughout much of the afternoon, producing golf ball-sized hail in Syracuse and spawning a very brief EF1 tornado in Verona Mills, which primarily caused damage to trees. Another tornado – this one being in Gilbertsville – caused significant damage to a school's athletic field.[39]
The second surface low corresponded to an area of strong upper level divergence ahead of the downstream shortwave. As the low formed across Texas and deepened while moving east, a tightening pressure gradient force further strengthened the low-level jet, therefore creating a broad warm sector across the southeastern states. This also generated stronger wind shear, providing better organization for the supercell storms as a result. Numerous tornadoes touched down across several states, including Texas, Louisiana, and Arkansas. Most of those tornadoes were weak, but a few of them caused considerable damage. A long-tracked wedge tornado caused EF2 damage in rural portions of Texas and Louisiana.[40] An EF3 tornado destroyed structures and caused severe damage at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, as well.[41] A total of 55 tornadoes were confirmed on the 26th, although no fatalities occurred.

April 27[edit]
